questions.question: Describe how a single movable pulley is rigged and explain, by considering the rope, why its mechanical advantage is 2.
questions.expected_answer: One end of the rope is fixed to a point above, the rope runs down round a pulley from whose block the load hangs, and back up to the effort on the free end; the pulley rises with the load. The load is supported by two rope sections, from the fixed point to the pulley and from the pulley to the effort. Being one continuous rope they have the same tension, and together they hold the load, so each carries half. The effort pulls on one section and so equals half the load; mechanical advantage is load over effort, which is 2, equal to the number of rope sections supporting the load.

questions.question: State the distance trade-off for a single movable pulley and show that work in equals work out.
questions.expected_answer: To raise the load by a distance, both supporting rope sections must shorten by that distance, so the free end must be pulled twice as far: 600 millimetres of rope for a 300 millimetre lift. Work in is effort times effort distance, half the load times twice the distance; work out is load times load distance; these are equal, less a little lost to friction. The movable pulley halves the force by doubling the rope pulled.

questions.question: Describe an investigation comparing a single fixed and a single movable pulley, state the expected results, and explain why the measured mechanical advantage of the movable pulley is below 2.
questions.expected_answer: With the same pulley and a 20 newton load, rig a fixed pulley and measure effort with a spring balance and rope pulled for a 300 millimetre lift: about 20 newtons and 300 millimetres, mechanical advantage 1, effort downward. Rig a movable pulley with the same load: about 10 to 11 newtons and 600 millimetres, mechanical advantage about 1.8 to 2, effort upward. Repeat with 10 and 30 newton loads and tabulate load, effort, distances and mechanical advantage. The measured value is below the ideal 2 because the effort also lifts half the pulley block's own weight and overcomes axle friction; the ratio of actual to ideal advantage is the efficiency, which improves with heavier loads.
